title: Reading Between the Lines
keyIdea: Some answers are right there in the words: who did it, where and when. Other answers are not said, so you look for clues. Sand and a wave tell you the beach, even if the word beach is not there. A good guess joins a clue with what you already know, and it fits every clue. Then you prove it: point to the line that shows you are right.

kid: Read: Ben fed his dog Pip in the garden after school. Who fed Pip? Ben. Where? In the garden. When? After school. The answers are right there. Go back and find the words.
Now read: Mia dug in the sand. A wave got her feet wet. Where is Mia? It does not say! But sand and a wave are clues. You find them at the beach. So Mia is at the beach.

Clue plus what I know makes a good guess. The grass is wet and there are big puddles. I know rain makes puddles. So it rained. A guess must fit all the clues. It is not a hot, dry day, because the grass is wet.
Show how you know. Point to the words that prove it. Camels can go for days without a drink. That line proves a camel can make a long trip with little water.
adult: This is the start of reading comprehension in both national systems. The US standards ask Grade 3 readers to ask and answer questions to show understanding, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for answers (CCSS RL.3.1 and RI.3.1). The English National Curriculum asks Years 3 and 4 to draw inferences, such as characters' feelings, thoughts and motives, and to justify inferences with evidence from the text.

Teachers often split questions into two kinds. Literal or right-there questions have the answer stated in the words, usually who, what, where or when. Inference questions need the reader to join a text clue with background knowledge to reach something unstated. Many classrooms call this clue plus what I know equals my inference, and it works for stories and for information texts alike.

Common mistakes: guessing from the picture or from their own life instead of looking back at the words; giving a when phrase for a where question; making a guess no clue supports; keeping a guess that one clue contradicts; and quoting a line that is true but does not prove the answer. Ask your child which words told them, every time.

In the lab your child answers right-there questions by tapping words, hunts two clues to find an unstated place or time, builds clue plus what I know guesses, and taps the line that proves an answer in a short camel fact text. Every tap and drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: At bedtime, stop on a page and ask one right-there question (Who? Where?) and one clue question (How do you think she feels? What time of day is it?). After each answer, ask: Which words told you? Let your child point.

visual.caption: “Ben fed his dog Pip in the garden. Pip wagged his tail.” Is each answer right there, or do you need clues?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find right-there answers, hunt two clues for what is not said, join a clue with what you know, and prove an answer with the right line.

practice.prompt: “Zara swam in the sea on Sunday.” When did Zara swim?
practice.hint: When words tell a time. Find the time in the sentence.
practice.explain: On Sunday tells a time, so it answers when. In the sea is a place, so it answers where.

practice.prompt: Each clue question needs 2 clues. Ella answers {a} clue questions. How many clues does she find?
practice.hint: Count 2 clues for every question she answers.
practice.explain: {a} questions with 2 clues each make {=2*a} clues.

practice.prompt: “Dad put on his sun hat. He rubbed on sun cream.” What is the weather like?
choices: It does not say, so we cannot tell
practice.hint: The word sunny is not there. What do the sun hat and sun cream tell you?
practice.explain: A sun hat and sun cream are clues. You need them when it is sunny, so it is a sunny day.

practice.prompt: A story has {a} pages. Sam finds {b} clues on each page. How many clues does he find?
practice.hint: Add the clues page by page. Every page has the same number.
practice.explain: {a} pages with {b} clues each make {=a*b} clues.

pool.prompt: “Kim fed the ducks at the pond.” Where did Kim feed the ducks?
pool.explain: At the pond names a place. The answer is right there in the words.

pool.prompt: “Raj put on his pyjamas and brushed his teeth. He yawned.” What time of day is it?
pool.hint: When do you put on pyjamas and yawn?
pool.explain: Pyjamas, brushing teeth and a yawn are clues. They all fit bedtime.

pool.prompt: “The floor was covered in mud. Muddy paw prints went to the dog bed.” Who made the mess?
choices: Nobody, the mud fell from the sky
pool.hint: Look at the paw prints. Where do they go?
pool.explain: Paw prints going to the dog bed are the clue, so the dog made the mess.

pool.prompt: Text: “Penguins cannot fly. They use their wings to swim fast.” Which line proves a penguin is a good swimmer?
choices: They use their wings to swim fast.
pool.hint: Find the line about swimming. Is every choice in the text?
pool.explain: They use their wings to swim fast proves it. Penguins cannot fly is true but is about flying, and the cold line is not in the text.

pool.prompt: “The ice cream ran down Joe’s hand. Drips fell on his shoes.” What can you work out?
choices: It is hot, so the ice cream is melting
Joe does not like ice cream
pool.hint: Clue: drips. What do I know about ice cream in the heat?
pool.explain: The drips are the clue, and I know ice cream melts in the heat. A freezing day goes against the clue.

pool.prompt: Why do you go back to the text after you answer?
choices: To find the words that prove it
pool.hint: How do you show someone your answer is right?
pool.explain: Good readers point to the words that prove their answer. That stops a wild guess.

pool.prompt: A text has {a} lines. Only 1 line proves the answer. How many lines do not prove it?
pool.hint: Take away the 1 line that proves it.
pool.explain: {a} lines take away 1 proving line leaves {=a-1} lines that do not prove it.

pool.prompt: Ali asks {a} right-there questions and {b} clue questions about a story. How many questions does he ask?
pool.hint: Add the two kinds of question together.
pool.explain: {a} right-there questions and {b} clue questions make {=a+b} questions.

pool.prompt: “Nia’s cheeks were red. She held her coat tight in the cold wind.” Which guess does NOT fit the clues?
choices: Nia is on a warm beach
pool.hint: Check each guess against every clue.
pool.explain: A warm beach goes against the cold wind clue. The other two guesses fit every clue.
